abstract: We introduce Fish Audio S2, an open-sourced text-to-speech system featuring multi-speaker, multi-turn generation, and, most importantly, instruction-following control via natural-language descriptions. To scale training, we develop a multi-stage training recipe together with a staged data pipeline covering video captioning and speech captioning, voice-quality assessment, and reward modeling. To push the frontier of open-source TTS, we release our model weights, fine-tuning code, and an SGLang-based inference engine. The inference engine is production-ready for streaming, achieving an RTF of 0.195 and a time-to-first-audio below $100\,\text{ms}$. Our code and weights are available on GitHub and Hugging Face. We highly encourage readers to visit https://fish.audio to try custom voices.

sections.body: The section motivates controllable text-to-speech and says the model keeps an earlier design while adding two changes: a data pipeline whose quality and transcription models are reused as reinforcement-learning rewards, and a GRPO variant that jointly optimizes semantic accuracy, acoustic quality and speaker similarity. Reported results are a posterior mean of 0.483 on the Audio Turing Test, rising to 0.515 with instruction rewriting, an overall win rate of 81.88% on Emergent TTS Eval, and an overall tag-activation rate of 93.3% on the new Fish Audio Instruction Benchmark, scored by Gemini 3 Pro. The section states no limitations.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Fine-grained speech control lacks training data at scale, so the report pairs a data pipeline with reinforcement-learning alignment.

sections.body: The audio tokenizer adapts the Descript Audio Codec to streaming at 44.1 kHz with ten residual vector quantization codebooks. Convolutions are causal, causal sliding-window Transformer blocks sit before and after the quantizer, and the encoder's total downsampling ratio is 2048, giving a frame rate of about 21 Hz. The decoder is EVA-GAN. The first codebook is trained with semantic distillation toward 16th-layer activations of w2v-BERT 2.0. For generation, a Qwen3-4B slow autoregressive model predicts the first codebook token each step, and a 4-layer fast model generates the nine remaining acoustic tokens. Their embeddings are summed into the next slow-model input. The section reports no limitations.
sections.heading: Architecture
sections.headline: The codec is streaming-capable, and generation splits a slow semantic model from a fast 4-layer acoustic model.

sections.body: Stage 1 separates vocals from background noise and uses voice activity detection to split audio into utterances. Stage 2 applies a speech quality model, trained on thousands of hours of human-labeled Stage 1 audio with a combined MSE and focal loss, to score signal-to-noise ratio, speaker consistency, recording quality and intelligibility, removing low-quality samples such as overlapping voices and residual music. Stage 3 uses a rich-transcription model fine-tuned from Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B. It transcribes speech, marks speaker turns, and inserts vocal instructions such as [prolonged laugh] and [inhale]. Training data came from video-based pseudo-labeling with human verification. The same two models later serve as RL rewards. The section reports no measurement of how filtering changes model quality.
sections.heading: Data Pipeline
sections.headline: Three-stage pipeline separates vocals, filters with a speech quality model, and annotates speech with a rich-transcription model, whose outputs also serve as rewards.

sections.body: The tokenizer has 446M parameters and is trained for 1M steps with a composite GAN loss over multi-period, multi-resolution and multi-scale STFT discriminators. Pre-training aligns audio tokens with Qwen3-4B in two stages, with context lengths of 8,192 and then 16,384 tokens, on over 10 million hours across about 80 languages and dialects, followed by supervised fine-tuning. Post-training samples a group of G candidates per prompt and uses group-mean advantages with no value network, following GRPO and Dr.GRPO. The total reward combines a speech-recognition reward that penalizes wrong speaker tags and missed instructions, a speech quality reward, and a voiceprint cosine similarity reward. LoRA with r=16 and alpha=64 on the MLP layers lets the reference policy sit in CPU memory. The section reports no limitations.
sections.heading: Training
sections.headline: Training runs in four stages, from a 446-million-parameter tokenizer through over 10 million hours of pre-training to reinforcement-learning post-training.

sections.body: Inference is built on SGLang, with three changes: an API-level bypass that skips the standard text tokenizer and detokenizer and streams acoustic token IDs; a RadixCache extended with multi-token keys so it can cache diverse reference audio contexts; and MPS co-scheduling of vocoder decoding with LLM decoding on the same GPU. On a single H200 GPU the section reports an RTF of 0.195 and time-to-first-audio as low as 100 ms in production. Under high concurrency it reports throughput of 3000+ acoustic tokens per second with RTF below 0.5. Reused voices reach an average prefix-cache hit rate of 86.4% and over 90% at peak. The section does not state the concurrency level behind the throughput figure.
sections.heading: Inference Engine
sections.headline: Streaming inference built on SGLang reaches an RTF of 0.195 and first audio in as little as 100 ms on one high-end accelerator.

sections.body: Objective metrics are word error rate (WER), character error rate (CER) and speaker similarity (SIM), plus an LLM judge for instruction following. On Seed-TTS-Eval, Fish Audio S2 scores 0.54 on test-zh, 0.99 on test-en and 5.99 on zh-hard, while CosyVoice 3-1.5B scores 5.83 on zh-hard. On the CV3-Eval subset, average error falls from 3.96 for Fish Audio S1 to 3.01, a 23.9% relative reduction. On Emergent TTS Eval, the overall win rate against the baseline is 81.88%, judged by Gemini 2.5 Pro, though its WER of 8.15 is not the lowest. The section states that MiniMax-Speech and ElevenLabs keep an advantage in some low-resource languages, and that Fish Audio S2 is only competitive on zh-hard.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: Fish Audio S2 reports the lowest error rate on Chinese and English voice-cloning benchmarks and in 11 of 24 languages on the multilingual testset.

sections.body: The conclusion restates three contributions: a Dual-AR architecture, a data pipeline in which the speech quality and rich-transcription models act as both pre-training filters and RL rewards, and RL post-training with multi-dimensional rewards for semantic accuracy, acoustic quality and speaker similarity. It cites evaluations on objective benchmarks and LLM-as-a-Judge benchmarks covering intelligibility, speaker similarity, naturalness and instruction following. It introduces the Fish Audio Instruction Benchmark and releases model weights, fine-tuning code and the SGLang-based inference engine. The section does not discuss limitations or future directions, although the introduction says Section 7 does.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The report concludes that its architecture, dual-purpose data pipeline and multi-reward RL support controllable, multi-speaker speech, and that weights and code are released.

sections.body: Core contributors, in order of contribution, are Shijia Liao, Yuxuan Wang, Songting Liu and Yifan Cheng. Other contributors are sorted by last name and then shuffled with Python 3.12 using random seed 42. They are listed as Ruoyi Zhang, Tianyu Li, Shidong Li, Yisheng Zheng, Xingwei Liu, Qingzheng Wang, Zhizhuo Zhou, Jiahua Liu, Xin Chen and Dawei Han. Correspondence is to oss@fish.audio. The section states no limitations.
sections.heading: Author
sections.headline: Core contributors are ranked by contribution, and the other contributors are shuffled with a fixed seed.

sections.body: The benchmark embeds word-level acoustic event tags, such as [laugh], [whispers], [inhale], [exhale] and [emphasis], in transcripts instead of using global style prompts. English samples come from the MELD dialogue corpus and Chinese samples from a community-curated game character voice corpus, each with about 500 utterances. Gemini 3 Pro scores three measures: Tag Activation Rate, the percentage of tags triggered at the exact position; acoustic naturalness on a 1–5 scale; and global expressiveness on a 1–5 scale. On 200 clips, Gemini 3 Pro agrees with human experts on acoustic-event detection 76.2% of the time, with Cohen's kappa of 0.47. Pearson correlations with human ratings are 0.55 for naturalness and 0.42 for expressiveness. The authors list limited data diversity, imbalanced tag distributions and early-stage alignment analysis as limitations.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix describes the Fish Audio Instruction Benchmark's construction, Gemini 3 Pro judging metrics, and its human-agreement checks.
